classification.difficultyReason: Develop and justify numerical invariants, investigate several finite dynamical systems, then find all ten-digit fixed points using a computer-assisted exhaustive strategy. The nonroutine search and completeness reasoning substantially exceed the supplied subtraction example.

questions.mappingNote: All five responses investigate the same repeated subtraction process. The supplied worked example remains visible; no recurrence-relation formalism is required.
questions.methodNote: The investigation supplies its own method: sort digits descending, reverse them, subtract and repeat while retaining leading zeros. External Chapter 1 page 2 supplies the subtraction interpretation.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Develop and justify numerical invariants, investigate several finite dynamical systems, then find all ten-digit fixed points using a computer-assisted exhaustive strategy. The nonroutine search and completeness reasoning substantially exceed the supplied subtraction example.

classification.difficultyReason: Combine binomial expansion and triangle areas to establish Pythagoras’ theorem geometrically.

questions.mappingNote: The directly assessed result is Pythagoras’ theorem; binomial expansion and triangle area are supporting skills. External Chapter 6 supplies distributive-law expansion, while Chapter 8 establishes the square-and-four-triangles area interpretation.
questions.methodNote: Expand the enclosing square’s area using the distributive law, calculate four times the right-triangle area, then equate the component areas and subtract 2ab.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Combine binomial expansion and triangle areas to establish Pythagoras’ theorem geometrically.

classification.difficultyReason: Evaluate three integer squares and compare the sum of the first two with the third.

questions.mappingNote: The task checks the complete triple 11, 60, 61 generated by the preceding example. All necessary numerical givens are retained in this question.
questions.methodNote: Evaluate the squares and compare their sum with the square of the hypotenuse, as in the displayed checks for 3, 4, 5 and 5, 12, 13.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Evaluate three integer squares and compare the sum of the first two with the third.

classification.difficultyReason: Apply a supplied multistep procedure to chosen starting values to generate Pythagorean triples.

questions.mappingNote: The closest supplied skill concerns Pythagorean triads; this task generates them using a numerical procedure rather than testing arbitrary triples.
questions.methodNote: Use the four-step odd-start procedure immediately preceding the task. The supplied example starts with 11 and produces 11, 60, 61. Positive odd starting values greater than 1 produce positive side lengths.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Apply a supplied multistep procedure to chosen starting values to generate Pythagorean triples.

classification.difficultyReason: Compare a supplied Pythagorean triple with the consecutive-side relationship imposed by the generation procedure.

questions.mappingNote: The response compares the supplied triple with this required difference of 1. The closest supplied skill concerns recognising and analysing Pythagorean triples.
questions.methodNote: The odd-number procedure constructs the second side by halving one less than the square of the starting number, then adds 1 to obtain the hypotenuse.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Compare a supplied Pythagorean triple with the consecutive-side relationship imposed by the generation procedure.

classification.difficultyReason: Apply the supplied multistep rule to generate integer side lengths.

questions.mappingNote: The task directly assesses substitution and evaluation in the supplied generation rule; the resulting numbers are Pythagorean triples.
questions.methodNote: Use Plato’s three-step procedure on page 13, demonstrated with starting side 8 on page 14: square the starting side, divide by 4, then subtract or add 1.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Apply the supplied multistep rule to generate integer side lengths.

classification.difficultyReason: Compare the structural restrictions of two procedures for generating Pythagorean triples.

questions.mappingNote: The question tests limitations of the two source procedures for generating Pythagorean triples. Converse of Pythagoras is the closest supplied catalogue skill.
questions.methodNote: Compare the difference between the generated hypotenuse and second side: 1 for Pythagoras’ procedure and 2 for Plato’s procedure.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Compare the structural restrictions of two procedures for generating Pythagorean triples.

classification.difficultyReason: Explain why both generating methods always give triples with no common factor greater than 1.

questions.mappingNote: The task asks for a general integer-factor explanation of both procedures, so proving results involving integers is the closest directly assessed skill.
questions.methodNote: Use the preceding Pythagoras and Plato generating procedures and the definition of primitive as having no common factor other than 1.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Explain why both generating methods always give triples with no common factor greater than 1.

classification.difficultyReason: Calculate six percentages from table data and verify ranking using premiership points before percentage.

questions.mappingNote: This activity directly assesses expressing one quantity as a percentage of another and interpreting tied positions in a table.
questions.methodNote: The introduction assigns four premiership points for a win and two for a draw. Divide points for by points against and multiply by 100%; place teams by premiership points first and percentage second.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Calculate six percentages from table data and verify ranking using premiership points before percentage.

classification.difficultyReason: Update supplied season totals from four results, compute percentages and sort with a stated two-level ranking rule; all procedures and table fields are explicit.

questions.mappingNote: The most advanced directly assessed calculation expresses goals for as a percentage of goals against. Updating and ordering the native ladder also assesses interpreting tabular data.
questions.methodNote: Page 14 supplies 4 points for a win and 2 for a draw. Page 15 defines percentage as goals for divided by goals against, multiplied by 100%, and ranks tied premiership-point totals by percentage. Activity 2 explicitly models adding the new scores to the season totals.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Update supplied season totals from four results, compute percentages and sort with a stated two-level ranking rule; all procedures and table fields are explicit.

classification.difficultyReason: Compare cumulative scoring percentages before and after a match and explain an unchanged ratio.

questions.mappingNote: The question assesses comparing a quantity as a percentage of another and explaining why adding proportional goals leaves the ratio unchanged. Page 15's initial scoring totals and all four sixth-round results are supplied within this question to make it independently answerable.
questions.methodNote: Page 14 introduces season scoring and ladder points. Page 15 defines percentage as goals for divided by goals against times 100%, then directs students to add sixth-round match scores to the season totals.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Compare cumulative scoring percentages before and after a match and explain an unchanged ratio.

classification.difficultyReason: Update cumulative scoring ratios and compare percentages before and after a win.

questions.mappingNote: The task assesses expressing one quantity as a percentage of another and interpreting changes in a sports table. The initial goals totals, percentage formula and all four sixth-round results are supplied from page 15 to make the assigned question self-contained.
questions.methodNote: Use cumulative goals for divided by cumulative goals against, multiplied by 100%. Add sixth-round scores to the five-game totals before comparing percentages. The source ladder and teacher table use one decimal place.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Update cumulative scoring ratios and compare percentages before and after a win.

classification.difficultyReason: Compare cumulative scoring percentages before and after a loss and identify a counterexample.

questions.mappingNote: The question directly assesses comparing one quantity as a percentage of another, using sporting totals and match results.
questions.methodNote: Use cumulative goals for divided by cumulative goals against, multiplied by 100%; update both totals with the sixth-round scores. The source uses percentages rounded to one decimal place.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Compare cumulative scoring percentages before and after a loss and identify a counterexample.

classification.difficultyReason: Update and total two related data columns, then explain why their totals agree.

questions.mappingNote: The assigned item assesses interpretation and totals of related table columns rather than calculation of percentages.
questions.methodNote: Page 15 updates each team's season goals by adding the goals scored and conceded in round six. Sum the updated columns and interpret the paired recording of every goal.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Update and total two related data columns, then explain why their totals agree.

classification.difficultyReason: Complete supplied quotient–remainder identities and transfer the same remainder into the explicitly scaffolded congruence notation.

questions.mappingNote: All four parts directly apply the division-and-remainder demonstrations. The catalogue's division–multiplication inverse skill is the closest match; it does not explicitly name modular arithmetic.
questions.methodNote: Write the dividend as modulus × whole-number quotient + remainder, with the remainder between zero and one less than the modulus; express that remainder in congruence notation.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Complete supplied quotient–remainder identities and transfer the same remainder into the explicitly scaffolded congruence notation.

classification.difficultyReason: Find a non-negative remainder for each supplied number and modulus.

questions.mappingNote: Each part directly applies the remainder interpretation of congruence taught on pages 16–18. Division with remainders is the closest supplied taxonomy skill.
questions.methodNote: Write the integer as modulus × quotient + remainder, using a whole-number remainder less than the modulus, then express the result as a congruence.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Find a non-negative remainder for each supplied number and modulus.

classification.difficultyReason: Find the least number above a bound with a specified remainder by choosing a suitable multiple.

questions.mappingNote: Each part selects the first multiple-plus-one above 50 and checks that the preceding such integer is at most 50. Connecting division and multiplication is the closest supplied catalogue skill. Neither reuse candidate has the same original task.
questions.methodNote: Pages 16–17 express integers as a multiple of the modulus plus a remainder. Page 18 explains that integers congruent to a remainder are that remainder more than a multiple of the modulus.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Find the least number above a bound with a specified remainder by choosing a suitable multiple.

classification.difficultyReason: Identify that the alternating phrases repeat every two petals and interpret the odd remainder47 mod2. One direct cycle interpretation.

questions.mappingNote: The two alternating phrases form a cycle of length 2. Remainder 1 identifies the first phrase. Interpret remainders is the closest supplied catalogue skill. Neither reuse candidate represents this original task.
questions.methodNote: Divide by the cycle length and interpret the remainder, following the days-of-the-week, finger-counting and clock examples. Modulo 2 has remainders 0 and 1.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Identify that the alternating phrases repeat every two petals and interpret the odd remainder47 mod2. One direct cycle interpretation.

classification.difficultyReason: Interpret the remainder after division by six as a position in a repeating alphabetical cycle.

questions.mappingNote: The remainder 2 in division of 80 by 6 identifies the second child, Bessie. Neither supplied reuse candidate represents this complete source task.
questions.methodNote: Divide by the cycle length and interpret the remainder, following the modulo 7 day-of-the-week examples and modulo 5 counting example. Here the six children form a repeating cycle.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Interpret the remainder after division by six as a position in a repeating alphabetical cycle.

classification.difficultyReason: Reduce a duration modulo 24 and interpret the remaining hours across midnight.

questions.mappingNote: This question directly applies the positive elapsed-hours clock method from page 16. Duration problems is the closest catalogue skill; interpreting remainders supports the modulo-24 calculation. Neither supplied reuse candidate has the same original task.
questions.methodNote: Page 16 reduces elapsed hours modulo 24 and advances the clock by the remainder. Page 17 extends clock congruences to negative durations; page 18 explains congruence through differences that are multiples of the modulus.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Reduce a duration modulo 24 and interpret the remaining hours across midnight.

classification.difficultyReason: Apply a seven-day cycle to identify recurring dates and determine a weekday from an elapsed-day remainder.

questions.mappingNote: Both requests apply the taught seven-day cycle. Repeated addition of seven identifies all Wednesdays; dividing the 26 elapsed days by seven determines the weekday of 27 November. Neither supplied reuse candidate contains this original task.
questions.methodNote: Use arithmetic modulo 7 for weekdays: complete weeks leave the weekday unchanged, and the remainder gives the remaining day shift.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Apply a seven-day cycle to identify recurring dates and determine a weekday from an elapsed-day remainder.

classification.difficultyReason: Apply a four-year calendar cycle and account for the century exception at 1900.

questions.mappingNote: Question 8 applies a calendar cycle to identify years one year before a leap year. Interpret remainders is the closest supplied skill; neither reuse candidate contains this original task.
questions.methodNote: The teaching interprets repeating calendar cycles using remainders and congruence. Apply the four-year leap-year cycle with the standard century exception.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Apply a four-year calendar cycle and account for the century exception at 1900.

classification.difficultyReason: Recognise that the last two digits determine each remainder because every modulus divides 100.

questions.mappingNote: Each modulus divides 100, so removing the leading multiple of 100 preserves the remainder. The closest catalogue skill is divisibility tests, supported by interpreting remainders. Neither supplied reuse candidate matches this complete task.
questions.methodNote: Use the division-with-remainder representation and congruence notation from pages 16–17, together with page 18's criterion that congruent integers differ by a multiple of the modulus.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Recognise that the last two digits determine each remainder because every modulus divides 100.

classification.difficultyReason: Identify the repeating cycle in time, weekdays and quarter-turns, then interpret the remainder.

questions.mappingNote: Part a uses a 24-hour cycle; b uses a seven-day cycle; c applies the same remainder method to the four quarter-turns in a full rotation. Interpreting remainders is the closest supplied catalogue skill. Neither supplied reuse candidate has the same original task.
questions.methodNote: Page 16 teaches division with remainder for repeating weekday and clock cycles. Pages 17–18 extend congruence and explain that whole cycles preserve the position in a cycle.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Identify the repeating cycle in time, weekdays and quarter-turns, then interpret the remainder.

classification.difficultyReason: Choose the negative quotient giving a nonnegative remainder, then construct two related number-line classes across negative and positive values; the scaffold links the representations.

questions.mappingNote: Part a applies the negative-integer division method; b translates its remainder into congruence notation; c applies the taught number-line representation with spacing 5. Neither supplied reuse candidate represents this complete task.
questions.methodNote: Page 17 expresses negative integers as a multiple of the modulus plus a nonnegative remainder. Page 18 marks multiples and congruent integers together on a number line and explains that congruent integers differ by a multiple of the modulus.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Choose the negative quotient giving a nonnegative remainder, then construct two related number-line classes across negative and positive values; the scaffold links the representations.

classification.difficultyReason: Construct two residue classes across the negative and positive interval, preserving the specified mod5 remainders. Routine number-line representation with negative members.

questions.mappingNote: Both parts apply the taught number-line method with modulus 5. The closest catalogue skill connects divisor, quotient and remainder; negative-integer arithmetic supports locating the points. Neither supplied reuse candidate contains this original task.
questions.methodNote: Use non-negative remainders for negative integers. Page 18 represents congruence classes on a number line by locating integers a fixed remainder above multiples of the modulus.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Construct two residue classes across the negative and positive interval, preserving the specified mod5 remainders. Routine number-line representation with negative members.

classification.difficultyReason: The supplied quotient-plus-remainder scaffold leads directly to each negative integer residue; repeated six calculations require no additional strategy beyond the taught nonnegative remainder.

questions.mappingNote: All six parts apply the demonstrated negative-integer division identity. The closest catalogue skill is connecting division and multiplication; neither supplied reuse candidate matches this complete task.
questions.methodNote: Write each integer as modulus times an integer plus a remainder from zero to one less than the modulus. Page 17 demonstrates this for negative integers; page 18 confirms the unique non-negative remainder convention.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: The supplied quotient-plus-remainder scaffold leads directly to each negative integer residue; repeated six calculations require no additional strategy beyond the taught nonnegative remainder.

classification.difficultyReason: Express positive and negative integers as divisor times integer quotient plus nonnegative remainder, then identify equal-remainder groups.

questions.mappingNote: Both parts explicitly require division followed by congruence classification. Page 17 supplies negative-integer division examples; pages 17–18 connect equal remainders with congruence. The supplied reuse candidates contain different complete tasks and cannot be reused.
questions.methodNote: Write each integer as modulus times an integer quotient plus a remainder from zero to one less than the modulus. For negative integers, use a negative quotient that leaves a nonnegative remainder. Integers with the same remainder are congruent.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Express positive and negative integers as divisor times integer quotient plus nonnegative remainder, then identify equal-remainder groups.

classification.difficultyReason: Check modular products by multiplying first and expressing each product as a multiple of the modulus plus a non-negative remainder.

questions.mappingNote: The task directly checks the multiplication method demonstrated on page 20. Pages 16–18 explain remainders and congruence, including negative integers. Connecting divisor, quotient and remainder is the closest supplied catalogue skill.
questions.methodNote: Multiply the original integers first, then write the product as modulus times an integer plus a remainder between zero and one less than the modulus. Compare that remainder with the supplied congruence.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Check modular products by multiplying first and expressing each product as a multiple of the modulus plus a non-negative remainder.

classification.difficultyReason: Reduce several addends modulo the given number and compare two methods in selected parts.

questions.mappingNote: The closest catalogue skill is division with remainders. Every part assesses addition of residues; parts a, b, c, d and g additionally require direct-addition comparison. Part h uses the congruent representative −1 to simplify the repeated sum.
questions.methodNote: Page 20 teaches replacing addends by congruent remainders, adding and reducing again, then checking by adding the original integers first. Pages 16–18 establish residues and congruence, including negative representatives.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Reduce several addends modulo the given number and compare two methods in selected parts.

classification.difficultyReason: Choose reduced representatives and compare reduction-first with multiplication-first for the indicated parts; linked routine computation rather than a new congruence proof.

questions.mappingNote: Question 2 directly applies the multiplication demonstrations on pages 20–21. The closest supplied catalogue skill connects products, divisors and remainders; efficient multiplication is secondary.
questions.methodNote: Reduce each factor modulo the stated modulus, multiply the remainders, then reduce the product. Check specified calculations by multiplying the original integers first.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Choose reduced representatives and compare reduction-first with multiplication-first for the indicated parts; linked routine computation rather than a new congruence proof.

classification.difficultyReason: Reduce several factors and successive products modulo a given integer.

questions.mappingNote: The closest supplied skill connects division, multiplication and remainders. The task directly assesses applying remainders to successive products.
questions.methodNote: Reduce factors to their remainders, multiply, and reduce successive products; multiplication is treated as repeated addition.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Reduce several factors and successive products modulo a given integer.

classification.difficultyReason: Group repeated factors and reduce intermediate powers modulo the given integer.

questions.mappingNote: Numerical index laws are the closest catalogue match for all eight parts; modular reduction additionally uses the quotient–remainder relationship.
questions.methodNote: Reduce factors modulo the modulus, group repeated factors into pairs or triples, and reduce intermediate products and powers.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Group repeated factors and reduce intermediate powers modulo the given integer.

classification.difficultyReason: Combine sums, products and powers while reducing intermediate results modulo the given integer.

questions.mappingNote: Question 5 combines the addition and multiplication methods on page 20 with repeated multiplication and grouped powers on page 21. The closest catalogue skill is integer order of operations, supported by powers and interpreting remainders.
questions.methodNote: Reduce operands modulo the modulus, calculate sums and products using their remainders, and reduce intermediate products when evaluating powers.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Combine sums, products and powers while reducing intermediate results modulo the given integer.

classification.difficultyReason: Calculate four modular sums and explain the general divisibility result they illustrate.

questions.mappingNote: The explanation generalises the four calculations to a divisibility result for integers; prove-results-integers is the closest supplied catalogue skill.
questions.methodNote: Add integers or their remainders, then reduce the sum modulo the stated modulus. Repeated addition is multiplication.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Calculate four modular sums and explain the general divisibility result they illustrate.

classification.difficultyReason: Interpret a remainder in a six-function cycle and determine the additional presses needed to complete it.

questions.mappingNote: The six-function watch is a repeating cycle analogous to the clock and weekday examples. Interpreting the remainder is the closest supplied catalogue skill.
questions.methodNote: Reduce the number of presses modulo the cycle length. Use addition of remainders to reach remainder zero, which represents the starting function.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Interpret a remainder in a six-function cycle and determine the additional presses needed to complete it.

classification.difficultyReason: Reduce the number of revolutions modulo 24, multiply the remainders and interpret the elapsed time on a clock.

questions.mappingNote: Interpret remainders is the closest supplied skill: the assessed task combines modular multiplication with interpreting a clock-time remainder.
questions.methodNote: Clock times repeat modulo 24. Reduce factors before multiplying, then reduce the product to its remainder, following the multiplication examples on pages 20–21 and clock examples on pages 16–17.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Reduce the number of revolutions modulo 24, multiply the remainders and interpret the elapsed time on a clock.

classification.difficultyReason: Combine four successive durations by adding their remainders modulo 7 and interpret the result as a weekday.

questions.mappingNote: Interpreting a remainder in a seven-day cycle is the closest supplied catalogue skill. The task also combines successive durations.
questions.methodNote: Use remainders modulo 7 for weekday cycles. Page 20 teaches reducing each duration before addition and reducing the resulting sum again; its calendar examples advance the starting weekday by the resulting remainder.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Combine four successive durations by adding their remainders modulo 7 and interpret the result as a weekday.

classification.difficultyReason: Reduce both factors modulo 5 and interpret the product's remainder as a position in a repeating finger cycle.

questions.mappingNote: This question applies modular multiplication to a five-position cycle. Interpreting remainders is the closest supplied catalogue skill; no dedicated modular-arithmetic skill was supplied.
questions.methodNote: Page 16 models counting repeatedly on five fingers using residues modulo 5. Pages 20–21 teach reducing factors before multiplying modulo the cycle length.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Reduce both factors modulo 5 and interpret the product's remainder as a position in a repeating finger cycle.

classification.difficultyReason: Combine three repeated rotations and interpret their remainder modulo 360.

questions.mappingNote: The repeated rotations use the multiplication and addition methods on pages 20–21, with a full turn supplying modulus 360. Interpreting the resulting remainder is the closest supplied catalogue skill.
questions.methodNote: Interpret congruence as a remainder; reduce products and add their remainders, reducing the resulting sum again when necessary.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Combine three repeated rotations and interpret their remainder modulo 360.

classification.difficultyReason: Connect modular powers, decimal place value and divisibility to prove three general statements.

questions.mappingNote: Part a applies the powers rule to 10 modulo 9. Part b applies that result to decimal place values and combines terms using multiplication and addition. Part c uses the definition of congruence and the fact that every multiple of 9 is a multiple of 3.
questions.methodNote: Use congruence as divisibility of the difference, reduce factors before multiplying, add congruent remainders, and take powers by repeated multiplication.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Connect modular powers, decimal place value and divisibility to prove three general statements.

classification.difficultyReason: Generalise the parity of powers of10 modulo11 and use a symbolic decimal expansion to prove the alternating-digit-sum claim for every whole number; part(a) scaffolds but does not supply the general proof.

questions.mappingNote: Part a applies the taught powers rule to 10 congruent to −1 modulo 11. Part b combines that result with decimal place value and the taught addition and multiplication rules. General integer proof is the closest catalogue skill.
questions.methodNote: Use congruent integers whose difference is a multiple of the modulus; reduce factors before multiplying or taking powers, and add congruent terms.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Generalise the parity of powers of10 modulo11 and use a symbolic decimal expansion to prove the alternating-digit-sum claim for every whole number; part(a) scaffolds but does not supply the general proof.

classification.difficultyReason: Apply the explicitly taught modular recurrence repeatedly, identify zero spacing and return of the starting consecutive pair, and report both patterns. Long repetition does not itself raise strategic demand.

questions.mappingNote: All nine parts apply the page-21 recurrence with a different printed modulus. The closest catalogue skill is recurrence-relation-definition; interpreting remainders supports the modular calculation. Repetition is confirmed by the return of the consecutive starting pair 1,1.
questions.methodNote: Page 21 defines the Fibonacci sequence with initial terms 1,1 and each subsequent term the sum of the preceding two, reduced modulo the chosen modulus. Its modulo-8 example distinguishes zero spacing from the full sequence period. Pages 16–18 define remainders and congruence; page 20 teaches addition of remainders.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Apply the explicitly taught modular recurrence repeatedly, identify zero spacing and return of the starting consecutive pair, and report both patterns. Long repetition does not itself raise strategic demand.
